QUOTES: Ahmed Zewail was born in Damanhour, grew up in Desouq and studied at Alexandria University. He kept going until he won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1999. Starting at an ordinary public school didn't stop him.
Taha Hussein lost his sight as a child, yet became the “Dean of Arabic Literature” and Minister of Education. He said education must be a right for everyone, like water and air.
Egyptian heart surgeon Magdi Yacoub performed thousands of operations around the world, then came back to build the Aswan Heart Centre. Mastery starts with daily repetition.
Naguib Mahfouz worked a day job and wrote every day at fixed hours, without waiting for the mood. That discipline took him to the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988.
As a boy, Mohamed Salah travelled for hours every day from Nagrig to train in Cairo. That long road is what made the player.
Sameera Moussa was one of Egypt's first women nuclear scientists. Her father moved the family to Cairo so she could continue her education, and she didn't let him down.
Michael Jordan didn't make his school's varsity team one year. He went home and cried, then trained harder than anyone and became one of the greatest basketball players ever.
J. K. Rowling's “Harry Potter” was rejected by many publishers before one accepted it. If she had quit after the first rejection, no one would know her name.
Marie Curie worked in a simple lab with few resources, and became the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences: physics and chemistry.
Ibn al-Haytham wrote the “Book of Optics” on light and vision while living in Cairo, and he is seen as one of the first to rely on experiment in science.
Mostafa Mosharafa was among the top students in the country, and became a physics professor and dean of the Faculty of Science while still young. He said science must reach people.
Thomas Edison tried a huge number of materials before finding one that worked for the light bulb. Every failed try brought him closer.
